name: ANZ Group Holdings Limited
overview: ANZ Group Holdings is one of Australia's "Big Four" banks and the number-one ranked bank in New Zealand, providing retail, commercial and institutional banking across Australia, New Zealand, the Pacific and Asia. Since the July 2024 acquisition of Suncorp Bank, ANZ is Australia's third-largest home lender, and the group is mid-way through a large-scale technology, culture and risk-management reset under CEO Nuno Matos (appointed May 2025) following an APRA court enforceable undertaking. ANZ.NZ is the NZX foreign-exempt listing of the same ASX-primary-listed entity (reports in AUD, fiscal year end 30 September; the NZX line itself quotes in NZD, last around NZ$45.17 on 7 August 2026 versus an ASX price near A$38.01); the H1-2026 (six months to 31 March 2026) result showed cash profit up 6% YoY as the cost-out programme and Suncorp integration began to flow through, and a Q3 FY2026 trading update/APS 330 disclosure is scheduled for 13 August 2026.

business_model.summary: ANZ earns the large majority of revenue from net interest income on loans (home loans, business/commercial lending, institutional lending) funded by customer deposits and wholesale funding, supplemented by fee, trading (Markets) and transaction banking income. Revenue is broadly recurring/spread-based (net interest margin of 1.53% cash on a ~$1.17 trillion average interest-earning asset base in H1-2026) rather than transactional, though the Institutional Markets business contributes more volatile trading income (~$1.1bn Markets income in H1-2026).

revenue_streams.name: Net interest income (Retail/Commercial/Institutional lending & deposits)
revenue_streams.trend: roughly flat YoY (Suncorp Bank now fully consolidated) with margin under ongoing pricing-competition pressure

revenue_streams.name: Markets (trading) income
revenue_streams.trend: stable to modestly growing (+3% YoY H1-2026) but inherently volatile

revenue_streams.name: Other (incl. equity-accounted associates)
revenue_streams.trend: recovering after FY2025 PT Panin impairment one-off

business_model.customer_type: Mix of B2C retail/mass-market (Australia Retail, Suncorp Bank, NZ Personal), B2B SME/commercial (Business & Private Bank, NZ Business/Agribusiness), and large corporate/institutional/government clients globally (Institutional division - Transaction Banking, Corporate Finance, Markets)
business_model.geographic_mix: Cash profit by division (H1-2026): Australia Retail $945m, Institutional $1,347m, New Zealand $788m, Business & Private Bank $698m, Suncorp Bank $258m, Pacific $29m, Group Centre -$285m; historically Australia contributes roughly half of Group cash profit, New Zealand around a quarter, and Institutional/Rest of World the remainder

competitive_position.market_position: Third-largest of Australia's Big Four by home lending post-Suncorp Bank acquisition; historically #1 ranked bank in New Zealand by market share, though ANZ NZ continued to lose home-loan market share through 2025 and into Q1 2026 as Kiwibank and ASB grew faster than their existing book share; a leading Institutional/corporate bank across Australia, NZ and Asia with a long-standing Asian and European network

moat_factors.description: Big Four Australian banks plus dominant NZ players control the vast majority of banking assets/deposits in a regulated, high-barrier-to-entry market; ANZ is #3 in Australian home loans post-Suncorp
APRA/RBNZ prudential licensing, capital and compliance requirements make new bank entry difficult, protecting incumbents despite intense internal competition

Differentiated pan-Asian and cross-border institutional franchise (Transaction Banking, trade, Markets) that smaller domestic peers cannot easily replicate; now full owner of the ANZ Worldline merchant-payments business (completed July 2026) after buying out Worldline's 51% stake for A$89m
Large, sticky customer deposit base (~$771B at March 2026, up 3% half-on-half) provides low-cost funding relative to wholesale markets

Historically strong brand, but repeated regulatory/conduct failures (bond-trading scandal, ASIC penalties, APRA CEU) have damaged trust; December 2025 Federal Court order finalised $250m in penalties, the largest combined ASIC penalty against a single entity, giving challengers/neobanks an opening

weaknesses: Weakest recent non-financial risk management track record among the Big Four, culminating in an APRA court enforceable undertaking and a $1bn operational risk capital add-on that remains in place
Continuing to lose NZ home-loan market share to Kiwibank and ASB through 2025 and into 2026, despite being NZ's largest bank

Cost-to-income ratio still elevated relative to Big Four peers even after H1-2026 improvement (49.4% cash H1-2026 vs 58.2% FY2025 average, which was inflated by Suncorp integration, restructuring and remediation costs)

Execution risk from simultaneous CEO transition, accelerated Suncorp Bank integration/migration, ANZ Plus rollout and NFR remediation, now compounded by growth-reacceleration pressure from investors/analysts (e.g., Goldman Sachs downgrade citing revenue headwinds)
Markets/trading income volatility can swing other operating income significantly period to period

Restructuring programme (~3,500 role reductions, ~1,000 contractor reductions) has drawn public and union criticism (Finance Sector Union) over pace and process, creating near-term morale/execution risk during a period requiring careful Suncorp migration and remediation delivery

growth_drivers: Suncorp Bank integration - migrating customers onto ANZ's platform ahead of the accelerated June 2027 target (34% complete at March 2026, targeting ~57% by September 2026), with synergies tracking ahead of the original ~$500m p.a. run-rate target (full run-rate expected FY2029) and delivering an incremental ~$29m of H1-2026 productivity

Accelerated ANZ Plus digital platform rollout to all ~8 million retail customers by September 2027 (three years earlier than original plan), with ANZ Plus already the majority channel for new retail product sales

Cost/productivity programme - FY2026 gross cost savings guided at ~$800-875m, with more than half of the ~3,500 planned role reductions and ~1,000 contractor reductions already completed by end-2025 (restructuring costs of ~$560m pre-tax), driving cost-to-income below 50% (cash) in H1-2026

CEO Nuno Matos's two-phase ANZ 2030 strategy ("get the basics right" FY2026-27, then growth investment), with a single customer front-end initiative unifying Australia Retail, Commercial and Suncorp onto common technology
Full ownership of the ANZ Worldline merchant-payments business (completed July 2026) enabling greater control and integration of the payments/transaction-banking value chain
Institutional franchise leverage of Asia trade/investment flows amid supply-chain diversification and geopolitical realignment (transaction banking, trade finance)

Capital normalisation and potential resumption of buybacks/higher payout as CET1 build, remediation progress and RBNZ's less onerous-than-feared final capital settings (adopted December 2025) reduce regulatory drag

business.description: ANZ NZ's home-loan share continued to slip through 2025 and Q1 2026 as Kiwibank (lending at roughly twice its book-share rate) and ASB gained share; increasing NZ competitive intensity could further pressure NZ margins/share

Accelerated migration timeline (brought forward to June 2027) reduces medium-term uncertainty as delivery has so far tracked ahead of plan, but continued execution and cost risk remains if delivery slips or customer attrition occurs during transition

Cost-out has driven the recent earnings improvement, but investors/analysts (e.g., Goldman Sachs Neutral downgrade) are increasingly focused on whether ANZ can sustain cost discipline while reaccelerating revenue growth once the productivity programme matures
Institutional Markets income remains inherently volatile period to period (total Markets income $1,108m in H1-2026, +3% YoY but with underlying swings across Rates, Credit, Commodities and FX)

Total credit impairment charge rose to 0.07% of average gross loans in H1-2026 (from 0.04% in H1-2025) and collectively assessed provisions/coverage continue to build, signalling gradual, early-stage normalisation from a benign base rather than acute stress

Public and union (Finance Sector Union) criticism of the pace and process of the ~4,500 role/contractor reductions could raise attrition of critical staff, employee-relations disputes or delivery risk during a period requiring precise Suncorp migration and remediation execution

financial.description: Group cash NIM fell to 1.53% in H1-2026 from 1.56% a year earlier, driven by asset pricing competition, lower NZ/international cash rates on deposit pricing, and Markets activity mix, partly offset by capital/replicating-portfolio tailwinds

APRA's operational risk capital add-on remains at $1 billion (raised from $750m in January 2026) and stays in place until remediation is delivered to APRA's satisfaction, permanently tying up capital that could otherwise support growth or shareholder returns

H1-2026 payout ratio ~68.5% (cash ~66.2%) is elevated versus historical Big Four norms; cash ROTE (11.6% H1-2026, up 161bps YoY) needs to sustain to support the current dividend and any resumed buybacks (the prior on-market buyback remains ceased)

Reported earnings affected by AUD/NZD and AUD/USD movements via economic hedging and NZ segment translation; ANZ flagged an expected ~$210m FX translation benefit to FY2026 cost guidance if rates hold near H1-2026 averages

regulatory.risk: APRA Court Enforceable Undertaking / Root Cause Remediation Plan
regulatory.description: April 2025 CEU with APRA over non-financial risk management and risk culture failures remains in force; the Root Cause Remediation Plan (RCRP) was submitted and accepted by APRA in September 2025 and the PACT programme is reported on track, but the $1bn capital add-on stays until remediation is delivered to APRA's satisfaction, and further sanctions/capital penalties remain possible if delivery slips

Federal Court finalised orders in December 2025 totalling $250 million in penalties (up from the initially agreed $240m after the Court added $10m on one matter) - the largest combined ASIC penalty against a single entity - covering Markets and Retail conduct matters affecting roughly 65,000 retail customers; financial impact is largely covered by existing provisions, but reputational damage persists and further legacy conduct issues could still surface

regulatory.risk: NZ Commerce Commission market study follow-through
regulatory.description: ANZ is implementing Commerce Commission recommendations (open banking acceleration) from the NZ personal banking competition study; the RBNZ's December 2025 final decision on its capital review adopted a modestly higher-than-2019 (but lower-than-status-quo) capital regime, which ANZ NZ welcomed as reducing upward pressure on lending rates versus the prior settings, with the next scheduled increase in NZ capital requirements from 1 July 2026

regulatory.risk: Bank levies and prudential capital changes
regulatory.description: Ongoing major bank levy (~$230m per half in H1-2026) and further RBNZ policy consultation on LAC requirements expected in H2-2026, alongside the next scheduled increase in NZ capital requirements from 1 July 2026

macro.description: The RBA has largely paused its easing cycle with inflation still above target (cash rate around 4.35% through mid-2026), while the RBNZ cut the OCR to 2.25% by late 2025 to support a fragile NZ recovery; divergent and uncertain rate paths in ANZ's two home markets create asset/deposit repricing and margin uncertainty

macro.risk: Australian/NZ household leverage and housing market
macro.description: High household debt-to-income levels in Australia/NZ leave mortgage books sensitive to unemployment shocks or house price declines
US tariff policy, US-China rivalry and supply-chain decoupling create volatility for ANZ's trade-finance and institutional Asia franchise
ANZ Research's FY2025 outlook flagged 2025 global growth (~3.2%) as the weakest since pandemic-affected 2020, with below-trend growth in many advanced economies continuing into 2026

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian and NZ banking is a mature, oligopolistic, heavily regulated industry; NZ Commerce Commission-driven structural reforms (open banking, switching ease) continue to increase competitive intensity, while in Australia mortgage/deposit price competition remains intense; RBNZ's December 2025 capital review outcome (a moderately higher, but less onerous than status quo, capital regime) was welcomed by ANZ NZ as reducing pressure on lending rates
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately cyclical - earnings sensitive to credit growth, net interest margin, and credit impairment charges through the economic cycle; less discretionary-consumer-exposed than retailers but exposed to housing and business credit cycles; H1-2026 shows early-stage, gradual credit normalisation off a benign base rather than acute stress
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - net interest margin, deposit/loan repricing dynamics, and the replicating portfolio/capital hedge all directly affected by RBA/RBNZ rate settings and yield curve shape; RBA and RBNZ rate paths have diverged, with Australia on hold near 4.35% and NZ cutting to 2.25% by late 2025
key_input_costs: Technology and platform investment (ANZ Plus, Suncorp migration)
Personnel costs and regulatory/compliance remediation spend

recent_developments.event: Q3 FY2026 trading update and APS 330 Pillar 3 capital/credit-quality disclosure due 13 August 2026 - the next scheduled market update after H1-2026 results; not yet released as of this analysis date

ANZ.NZ traded around NZ$45.17 on the NZX (7 August 2026) versus an ASX price near A$38.01 (up ~1.9% intraday, ~25% higher over the trailing year); market capitalisation approximately A$114.4bn; dividend yield around 4.4%, above the ASX diversified-banks average

ANZ completed its acquisition of Worldline's 51% stake in the ANZ Worldline merchant-payments joint venture for A$89m, taking full ownership of the merchant payments business (approval-conditional deal announced May 2026)

H1-2026 results: statutory profit flat YoY at $3,650m, cash profit up 6% to $3,780m (up 14% ex significant items vs prior half); cash ROTE up 161bps to 11.6%; CET1 ratio 12.4% (up 36bps half-on-half); cost-to-income (cash) improved to 49.4%; interim dividend held at 83 cents per share with franking raised to 75%; remaining prior on-market buyback stayed ceased

Suncorp Bank customer migration programme 34% complete against the accelerated June 2027 full-migration target, tracking toward ~57% completion by September 2026; synergies reported ahead of original expectations, with full run-rate synergies now expected in FY2029

APRA increased ANZ's operational risk capital add-on from $750m to $1 billion and formally accepted the Court Enforceable Undertaking, confirming the sanction remains until remediation is delivered to APRA's satisfaction

RBNZ finalised its 2025 review of bank capital settings, adopting a moderately higher (vs 2019) but lower-than-status-quo capital regime; ANZ NZ welcomed the outcome as reducing upward pressure on lending rates. Separately, the Federal Court finalised ASIC penalty orders against ANZ totalling $250 million (up from the initially agreed $240m), covering roughly 65,000 affected retail customers across Markets and Retail conduct matters

FY2025 full-year results: statutory profit down $560m (-8.5%) to $6,035m; cash profit down 13% to $5,931m; cost-to-income ratio (cash) rose to 58.2% from 51.3% on Suncorp integration, restructuring, ASIC-settlement and PT Panin impairment one-off charges

ANZ 2030 Strategy Day: CEO Nuno Matos and CFO Farhan Faruqui announced acceleration of Suncorp Bank migration to June 2027 and ANZ Plus rollout to all 8 million retail customers by September 2027; upgraded FY2026 cost-reduction and productivity-savings guidance

ANZ submitted the Root Cause Remediation Plan (RCRP) to APRA under the CEU; announced ~3,500 planned employee departures and ~1,000 fewer contractor engagements (restructuring cost of ~$560m pre-tax; roughly 8% of the ~42,000-strong workforce), drawing public and Finance Sector Union criticism over the pace and process of the cuts; entered ASIC settlement (~$240m penalties plus costs) covering Markets and Retail conduct matters; Cashrewards ceased offers as ANZ exits non-core non-bank activities
Nuno Matos formally became CEO and Executive Director (12 May 2025), succeeding long-serving CEO Shayne Elliott (2016-2025)
ANZ confirmed the Court Enforceable Undertaking with APRA and released the Oliver Wyman independent report into non-financial risk management and risk culture

guidance.as_of: H1-2026 Results (May 2026) and October 2025 Strategy Day

items.notes: Upgraded from an earlier ~3% reduction target off the FY2025 ~$11.85bn baseline (adjusted for significant items); H1-2026 already showed cash opex down 4% YoY and cost-to-income below 50%, ahead of the full-year run-rate implied by guidance
Up from a prior lower target; more than half of the ~3,500 planned role reductions completed by end-2025; plus an expected ~$210 million FX translation benefit if rates hold near H1-2026 averages

Brought forward from original later timeline at the October 2025 Strategy Day; 34% complete as of March 2026, targeting ~57% by September 2026; synergies tracking ahead of the original ~$500m p.a. run-rate target, with full run-rate synergies now expected in FY2029

items.target: All ~8 million retail customers migrated to ANZ Plus platform
items.notes: Three years earlier than the original plan; ANZ Plus is already the majority channel for new retail product sales

items.target: Maintain CET1 comfortably above regulatory minimum while absorbing APRA's $1bn operational risk capital add-on
items.notes: CET1 was 12.4% at March 2026, up from 12.0% at September 2025 and 11.8% at March 2025

items.target: No new buyback announced; prior on-market buyback remains ceased
items.notes: Board continues to prioritise capital build and remediation funding over further buybacks in the near term; interim dividend held flat at 83 cents with franking increased to 75%

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Nuno Matos has framed FY2026-27 as a 'get the basics right' phase within the two-phase ANZ 2030 strategy, with immediate priorities of resetting culture, integrating Suncorp Bank, building a single customer front-end, driving deep productivity improvements, and remediating non-financial risk matters, before a second phase shifts toward growth investment. Management says the Root Cause Remediation Plan was accepted by APRA in September 2025 and the PACT (People, Accountability, Customers, Trust) programme is on track. At the H1-2026 briefing, Matos and CFO Farhan Faruqui highlighted that the cost-out programme is running ahead of schedule (cost-to-income below 50% cash), Suncorp synergies are tracking ahead of plan, and capital position and provision coverage continue to strengthen, while flagging that investor and analyst attention is increasingly shifting toward whether ANZ can translate the cost discipline into sustainable revenue/earnings growth once productivity gains mature. The next scheduled disclosure is the Q3 FY2026 trading update/APS 330 release on 13 August 2026.

bull_case: Cost/productivity reset is running ahead of schedule under new CEO Nuno Matos - cost-to-income ratio fell below 50% (cash) in H1-2026 from the FY2025 Suncorp/remediation-inflated 58.2% peak, with FY2026 savings guidance upgraded to ~$800-875m

Suncorp Bank acquisition makes ANZ the #3 Australian home lender, with migration and synergy delivery tracking ahead of the accelerated June 2027 plan, and the ANZ Plus rollout could structurally lower the cost-to-serve across the retail base

H1-2026 results confirm the turn - cash profit up 6% YoY (+14% ex significant items), cash ROTE up 161bps to 11.6%, CET1 strengthened to 12.4% - with the FY2025 trough (restructuring charges, ASIC settlement, PT Panin impairment) now behind the company and full ownership of the ANZ Worldline payments venture adding a further integration lever

Diversified franchise across Australia, NZ, Pacific and Asia Institutional banking provides earnings resilience versus single-market peers, with a differentiated trade/Markets business, and RBNZ's finalised capital-review outcome was less onerous than the Commerce Commission had pushed for

Well-covered, growing-franking dividend (83 cents interim, ~66-69% cash payout ratio, ~4.4% yield) with potential for resumed buybacks once capital build and APRA remediation are further along; several analysts (e.g., Citi) rate the stock a Buy citing it as the pick of the Big Four
bear_case: APRA Court Enforceable Undertaking and ongoing Root Cause Remediation Plan represent multi-year execution risk and an unusually weak non-financial risk track record versus Big Four peers, with the $1bn capital add-on (increased from $750m in January 2026) a persistent drag on returns until APRA is satisfied remediation is complete

Cost cuts have driven the recent earnings recovery, but sustaining growth once the productivity programme matures is unproven - Goldman Sachs and other analysts have flagged revenue headwinds and downgraded the stock, and consensus rating is only 'Neutral' (14 analysts: 6 Buy, 6 Hold, 2 Sell) with price targets spanning roughly A$31.85-40.50 and an average near A$35.60

Continuing to lose NZ mortgage market share to Kiwibank/ASB despite being NZ's largest bank, and facing structural competitive reform (Commerce Commission-driven open banking, RBNZ capital changes effective July 2026) could further erode ANZ's historically strong New Zealand franchise

Net interest margin remains under pressure (1.53% cash in H1-2026, down from 1.56% a year earlier) from asset/deposit pricing competition and diverging RBA/RBNZ rate paths, while credit impairment charges (0.07% of average loans, up from 0.04%) and provisioning are gradually rising off a benign base, pointing to early-stage cyclical credit normalisation

Repeated conduct/regulatory failures culminated in the largest combined ASIC penalty ever levied against a single entity ($250m, finalised December 2025) covering ~65,000 affected retail customers, and the ~4,500 role/contractor reduction programme has drawn public and union backlash (Finance Sector Union disputes); reputational and execution risk could recur, with further fines, remediation costs, staff attrition, or share loss to challengers all possible
